newsitem.title: GERMANY: German jobs problem seen too deep for EU pact.
newsitem.headline: German jobs problem seen too deep for EU pact.

text.p: Whatever emerges from European summit negotiations in Amsterdam, German labour market experts are sceptical whether it could significantly help to cut record jobless levels in the continent's largest economy.

The core of the German problem, highlighted in last week's Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) report, is the residue of structural joblessness that does not go away even when the economy is looking up.

"What we've seen in Germany for some time now is that every time the economy has emerged from a recession, we've ended up with fewer jobs than at the start of the cycle," said Hermann Remsperger, chief economist at Frankfurt-based BHF Bank.

According to the Paris-based OECD, just 1.1 percent of unemployment within the German workforce can be attributed to cyclical economic reasons, while 9.8 percent is a result of the structure of the labour market itself.

This means that Germany stands to benefit much less from an economic upswing than say, France, where the OECD estimates that more than twice as much of the workforce is dependent on wider economic conditions.

As Chancellor Helmut Kohl acknowledged on two separate occasions in the past week, current German economic growth -- at a reasonable 2.5 percent a year -- may not be enough to help the government towards its goal of halving unemployment by the year 2000.
Views differ on why the structure of the German labour market appears unable to create new job opportunities.

Bonn's view, shared by many private sector economists, is that costly social state provision coupled with a collective bargaining process that has made German workers among the most affluent in the world is pricing German labour out of the market.
"The market must be made more flexible on the basis of the Anglo-Saxon model and the wage agreement process must be decentralised to take into account individual firms," BHF's Remsperger said.
But trade union and left-leaning analysts argue that the structural joblessness is the result of an unfair distribution of vast productivity gains made over the years.

"Look at the auto industry, where productivity has in some cases been rising at 10 percent a year. That's around four times the economic growth rate," said Johannes Jakob, labour market analyst for the German Trade union Federation (DGB).
Jakob, in line with other trade unionists, argued that a redistribution of productivity gains through reduced overtime work and shorter hours would give room for job creation.

But while he welcomed the greater coordination of national labour policies that is likely to be part of the EU Employment Chapter, he echoed Bonn's fears that Germany could end up being a net payer for any Brussels-led jobs programmes.
"If the EU ends up leading these projects, there's always the risk that Germany becomes the largest net payer, which is not the best solution for us," he said.

Jakob said Germany could potentially benefit from an Employment Chapter that promoted the development of venture capital and support of self-employed workers, but only if such schemes were managed nationally rather than from Brussels.
